text:
A law firm and several other companies have fallen into administration(Image: Getty Images)

It's been an extremely tough year already for British businesses, with thousands being forced to call in administrators. When this happens, the company is then run by an administrator, and control of its assets are handed over as well.

There are plenty of reasons why this might happen, but some of the most common ones are debt, soaring overhead costs, reduced sales and dwindling footfall. Some of the most recent companies to enter administration include a law firm, a school - which has now closed - and a housebuilding company.

Here's a roundup of the details that you might have missed recently.

Some business can't be saved by administrators and are forced to close(Image: Getty Images)

A high street law firm has collapsed into administration owing £2.5 million, leaving clients stranded and vital legal documents locked away.

BLB Solicitors, which operated offices in Bath, Swindon, and Bradford on Avon, shut its doors on April 30. The sudden closure left local families and businesses stumped as they tried to retrieve crucial documents, including house deeds and wills.

One former employee spoke out after the closure, branding the situation an 'absolute shambles' and noting that warning signs were clear weeks before the collapse.

While the firm saw a stable turnover of £4.56 million in 2023 and a brief recovery to £5.54 million in 2025, it ultimately buckled under financial pressures.

Administrators said it was down to a combination of a prolonged slowdown in property transactions, soaring staffing costs, key staff departures and issues with a new case management system.

By March 2026, cash flow pressures forced directors to seek insolvency advice, leading to the sudden shutdown just weeks later.

Agile Property and Homes, which specialised in building low-carbon, flat-pack sustainable homes across Bristol and Oxfordshire, appointed administrators on July 6.

The sudden collapse comes just seven years after the firm was founded, and only a year after chief executive Craig White claimed the business had the 'proven model to tackle the UK's housing crisis at low cost and speed.'

The firm was known for partnering with charities and housing associations to build affordable, natural-material homes in as little as 12 weeks.

However, joint administrator Andrew Pear, of Moorfields Advisory, said the business was ultimately derailed by a combination of soaring energy, labour and raw material costs.

He warned that the wider system is 'broken,' pointing to planning permission delays and a 'massive skills shortage' holding back developers.

The firm's collapse is another blow to the Government's target of building 1.5 million homes by 2029, with the industry currently predicted to fall short of its goals.

A housebuilder has also fallen into administration(Image: Bloomberg via Getty Images)

St Gerard’s School in Bangor was founded in 1915 by the Sisters of Mercy. However, after 111 years of operation, the school was forced to close permanently at the end of the summer term on July 3.

Trustees informed parents with a 'heavy heart' that the school could no longer survive under the huge financial pressures.

In a letter to families, school bosses blamed rising National Insurance costs, the loss of their charitable status, and the Labour government’s controversial decision to add 20% VAT on private school fees, as well as falling pupil numbers.

An official notice confirmed that the trust behind the school entered administration on its final day of term, with Simon Farr and Anthony Collier of FRP Advisory appointed to handle the closure.

The majority of staff have been made redundant, though a small crew remains to process exam results this summer and support affected families.

The closure has sparked a row, with Helen Jenner MS, Reform UK Wales’s deputy leader, slamming the decision to target independent schools as 'pure ideological spite,' warning it would pile pressure onto a state sector already struggling under stretched budgets.

Finally, this packaging firm has collapsed into administration, but a quick rescue deal has successfully saved more than 30 jobs.

Derwent Packaging Limited, which has built cardboard and retail displays for brands since 1994, entered administration on July 8. The Derbyshire-based business became the latest casualty of the financial squeeze, thanks to mix of rising labor costs, high energy bills and a drop in customer spending.

Official documents revealed the extent that these issues had affected the business. The firm's tangible assets dropped from £330,410 to £270,657 between 2024 and 2025, with cashflow issues eventually forcing the company to stop trading.

However, joint administrators Benjamin Fallon and Louise Longley, of Begbies Traynor, managed to pull off a full sale of the business within just 24 hours of being appointed.

The company has now been acquired by Mailway Displays, securing the future of the firm's manufacturing base in Denby, where it has operated for more than three decades.

Most importantly, the rescue deal means all 33 jobs at the site have been saved and customer orders will continue to be filled without disruption.
